components.explanation: Here is the whole loop, as resource text. One value track, path dot colon frame, on the sprite itself. Four keys, at zero, a third, two thirds and one second, with values zero, one, two and three. Update one is discrete, so the frame jumps instead of sweeping. Loop mode one is loop linear, and the length is sixteen twelfths of a second. This is Closure at the base store, in the running game, through a preview fixture that only places the player for framing. Each cell holds for a third of a second, ten capture frames. The last key sits one interval before the end, so the wrap from cell three back to zero takes exactly as long as every other step. The user watched it in the game and said: All fine.

Which picture is frame three? That isn't the image's business. The sprite's texture is the sheet, and h frames four, with one row, cuts it into four cells of sixty four pixels. The slicing decides which cell frame three names. The read-back test checks every key against h frames times v frames: nothing above three. Here is the actual sheet with its four cells numbered, and four capture frames, one per key. The picture in each frame is the cell the track named. Nothing in the clip knows it's Closure: the same clip, with another texture, breathes for the squad and the trader.

So what if a track names a property that doesn't exist? Godot plays the clip anyway. A track that points at nothing sets nothing, with no error. That's why the read-back resolves every track. For an ordinary track, this line asks whether the node has the named member. Bone and blend shape tracks branch off before it. Mutation one, in its own worktree, from an empty cache: the rig's arm rotation track renamed to rotaton, in the clip only. The read-back exits one, and the line says why: wave release track four, ArmFront has no property rotaton. In the game, that arm would just stop moving. Loop mode flipped to none, and a key set to cell four: also exit one.

One authority. Before this change, the field set pieces wrote each figure's frame directly, so the squad wouldn't breathe in step. That was a second writer on a node the Animation Player now owns. The same random draw is kept, but it becomes one seek of the figure's own clip, once it's in the tree. The Animation Player stays the only thing that writes frame. The field squad, in the same fixture run. The structure test read the three figures at a third, a third and two thirds of a second: not all in step. If two things wrote one sprite, whichever ran last in the frame would win, and that depends on node order, not on any design.

On the player, the release click starts the rig. The wave state machine writes the billboard's visibility and the rig root's facing, and it is the operator sprite's only visibility writer too, the same place that already hid it for Amiya's shadow skill. No clip keys those properties, so nothing fights it. In the user's strip, frame twenty seven, the click, is still the sprite. On twenty nine, the rig has replaced it, and on fifty the sprite is back. The film's scripted run logs the same swap: sprite hidden while the state is startup, active or recovery, shown again in ready.

Two clocks. An Animation Player can advance on the process tick or the physics tick. Gameplay reads the active window on the physics tick, so this rig runs in manual mode. Each physics tick that isn't frozen by hitstop, the same delta, times the attack speed rate, advances both the state machine's time and the clip. Frame six fires the wave from the state machine's own count, never from the clip. The structure test, through real input, records every tick. At rate one, active opens after twelve unfrozen ticks, recovery after twenty, ready after forty, and four hitstop ticks freeze both clocks together. At rate one and a half: eight, fourteen and twenty seven. Every tick, clip position equals the state machine's time, within a ten thousandth of a second. The NPC loop runs on the process tick, and nothing reads it.

Feel is designed in frames. The phase table says six startup frames, four active, ten recovery, at thirty frames a second, with a step of one thirtieth. So the arm's keys sit at zero, point two, a third, and two thirds of a second: frames zero, six, ten and twenty. Transition two eases into the sweep, and point five eases out through recovery. Here's the rig alone, in a fixture with nothing but a grey floor, stepped one thirtieth of a second per frame. The blades wind back through startup, swing through the active frames, and settle by frame twenty. The parts are cut unchanged from Lappland's combat sheet. Only their pivots move.

The state table in code: four states, the clip each one plays, and three transitions, at frames six, ten and twenty. A dodge or loss of control in any state goes back to ready, and a swing in recovery cuts it short. The structure test checks this table against the brief, and against the rig's own animation library. The user's Movie Maker capture, read at each boundary. Frame twenty nine is the first startup frame, two of them hitstop. Thirty six is the last startup frame. On thirty seven, the charge mark is gone, and the wave leaves. Forty one starts recovery, and on fifty the sprite is back. The user's verdict: I saw the record, everything is nice, we did a good job. Then: keep r zero, no revision.

The edges. For each boundary, a real dodge arrives one frame before it, on it, and one frame after. Before frame six: no wave, and the charge is kept. On or after six, the wave is already out. The test asserts exactly that: nine cases, thirty nine checks. A scripted input capture of the same rule in the running game: a real click, then a real dodge event, timed by reading the state. First, a full release. Then a dodge in startup: no wave, and the charge is kept. A dodge on the first active frame: the wave is already out. A dodge in recovery cuts the settle. Between takes, a ground click walks her back, and the charge is refilled as a fixture.
The two clips, their routes and nodes, which loops and which commits, and the authority over each.
Recorded results of the read-backs, pins, structure and edge tests, mutations and suites, and their headless limits.
Human checks, who did what, the sheet's source, the filmed revision and the verdict.

var phase := rng.randi_range(0, FieldArt.NPC_FRAMES - 1)
			# Standing upright, stretched by the camera's tilt so it draws the
			# same pixels: a camera-facing billboard leans back into the set piece
			# behind it and loses its head there.
			figure.billboard = BaseMaterial3D.BILLBOARD_FIXED_Y
			# (GmCamera._keep_sprites_upright stretches it again at another tilt.)
			figure.scale.y = GameManager.CAMERA_OFFSET.length() / absf(GameManager.CAMERA_OFFSET.z)
			figure.add_to_group("upright_figures")
			node.add_child(figure)
			var clip := figure.get_node("AnimationPlayer") as AnimationPlayer
			clip.seek(phase * clip.get_animation(&"idle").length / FieldArt.NPC_FRAMES, true)

func _wave_begin(direction: Vector3, target: Enemy, damage: float, crit: bool) -> void:
	wave_state = WaveState.STARTUP
	wave_frame = 0
	_wave_time = 0.0
	_wave_rate = animation_rate()
	_wave_pending = {"direction": direction, "target": target, "damage": damage, "crit": crit}
	swing_remaining = WAVE_END_FRAME / (WAVE_FPS * _wave_rate)
	if not is_instance_valid(_wave_player): return
	# The rig's parts face west (screen left); mirrored when she swings to the right.
	_wave_rig_root.scale.x = -1.0 if cos(_sprite._screen_angle(direction)) > 0.0 else 1.0
	_wave_viewport.render_target_update_mode = SubViewport.UPDATE_ALWAYS
	_wave_player.play(WAVE_CLIPS[WaveState.STARTUP])
	_wave_player.seek(0.0, true)
	_wave_billboard.visible = true
	_sprite.visible = false

tracks/2/path = NodePath("ArmBack:rotation")
tracks/2/interp = 1
tracks/2/loop_wrap = true
tracks/2/keys = {
"times": PackedFloat32Array(0, 0.2, 0.333333, 0.666667),
"transitions": PackedFloat32Array(2, 1, 0.5, 1),
"update": 0,
"values": [0.0, -0.7, 1.4, 0.0]
}

const WAVE_CLIPS := {
	WaveState.READY: &"RESET",
	WaveState.STARTUP: &"wave_release",
	WaveState.ACTIVE: &"wave_release",
	WaveState.RECOVERY: &"wave_release",
}
## [from, design frame, to]: the clock's transitions. Interrupts (dodge, loss
## of control, operator swap, death, leaving the field) and a swing in
## RECOVERY go to READY.
const WAVE_TRANSITIONS := [
	[WaveState.STARTUP, 6, WaveState.ACTIVE],
	[WaveState.ACTIVE, 10, WaveState.RECOVERY],
	[WaveState.RECOVERY, 20, WaveState.READY],
]

code_result_pairs.observation: This is Closure at the base store, in the running game, through a preview fixture that only places the player for framing. Each cell holds for a third of a second, ten capture frames. The last key sits one interval before the end, so the wrap from cell three back to zero takes exactly as long as every other step. The user watched it in the game and said: All fine.

Here is the actual sheet with its four cells numbered, and four capture frames, one per key. The picture in each frame is the cell the track named. Nothing in the clip knows it's Closure: the same clip, with another texture, breathes for the squad and the trader.

Mutation one, in its own worktree, from an empty cache: the rig's arm rotation track renamed to rotaton, in the clip only. The read-back exits one, and the line says why: wave release track four, ArmFront has no property rotaton. In the game, that arm would just stop moving. Loop mode flipped to none, and a key set to cell four: also exit one.

The field squad, in the same fixture run. The structure test read the three figures at a third, a third and two thirds of a second: not all in step. If two things wrote one sprite, whichever ran last in the frame would win, and that depends on node order, not on any design.

In the user's strip, frame twenty seven, the click, is still the sprite. On twenty nine, the rig has replaced it, and on fifty the sprite is back. The film's scripted run logs the same swap: sprite hidden while the state is startup, active or recovery, shown again in ready.

The structure test, through real input, records every tick. At rate one, active opens after twelve unfrozen ticks, recovery after twenty, ready after forty, and four hitstop ticks freeze both clocks together. At rate one and a half: eight, fourteen and twenty seven. Every tick, clip position equals the state machine's time, within a ten thousandth of a second. The NPC loop runs on the process tick, and nothing reads it.

Here's the rig alone, in a fixture with nothing but a grey floor, stepped one thirtieth of a second per frame. The blades wind back through startup, swing through the active frames, and settle by frame twenty. The parts are cut unchanged from Lappland's combat sheet. Only their pivots move.

The user's Movie Maker capture, read at each boundary. Frame twenty nine is the first startup frame, two of them hitstop. Thirty six is the last startup frame. On thirty seven, the charge mark is gone, and the wave leaves. Forty one starts recovery, and on fifty the sprite is back. The user's verdict: I saw the record, everything is nice, we did a good job. Then: keep r zero, no revision.

A scripted input capture of the same rule in the running game: a real click, then a real dodge event, timed by reading the state. First, a full release. Then a dodge in startup: no wave, and the charge is kept. A dodge on the first active frame: the wave is already out. A dodge in recovery cuts the settle. Between takes, a ground click walks her back, and the charge is refilled as a fixture.
